diff_user.system: You are optimizing a Go function. Popcount(xs []uint64) int must return the total number of set bits across all words of xs. Each candidate is scored by running it in giri, a Go SSA interpreter, on 50 test vectors. It must return the reference result on every vector, and leave xs unchanged. Among correct candidates, a lower abstract cost (the number of SSA instructions executed over all vectors) scores higher, and any correct candidate scores above any incorrect one. The only import allowed is math/bits. Keep the function's name and signature.
responses:
## Analysis

The last three attempts restructured the tail ladder, but each produced exactly the same cost (3567 vs. reference 7570) and the same fitness. That suggests the ladder's control flow is not where the cost is. The likely overhead is in the `xs[i]` index expressions: each constant index into a slice emits a runtime bounds check (a compare plus a branch) in SSA. The 16-word peel has 16 such checks per call.

Go lets you convert a slice to a fixed-size array pointer, `(*[16]uint64)(xs)`. This panics if `len(xs) < 16`, which the guard already rules out. Constant indices into an array pointer are checked at compile time, so the 16 per-word bounds checks disappear from the SSA. The only remaining runtime check is the one in the conversion, plus the one in `xs[16:]`. Output is unchanged, the input slice is not modified, and only `math/bits` is used.

This is a targeted change to the 16-word peel block only. The tail ladder stays as it is, so the risk of breaking correctness is limited to one block.
